title: He Left SpaceX to Rebuild the American Factory
summary: A single replacement part for one of the Air Force's most important cargo planes can take four years to build. A former SpaceX engineer just proved his robots can make one in two months.*How scrappy startups take on industries worth billions:* https://clickhubspot.com/nxmiEd Mehr left SpaceX and Relativity Space to solve a problem that had nothing to do with software: manufacturing can't move at software speed. His fix, Machina Labs, replaces the custom, million-dollar "dies" that traditional stamping relies on with two robotic arms that can shape sheet metal into almost anything — no new tooling required. It's already caught the attention of the US Air Force, NASA, and Lockheed Martin, who's betting on Machina to help diversify a defense supply chain where 87% of programs cite supply-chain issues as a bottleneck to scaling. The tradeoff is speed — Machina can't out-produce a stamping line yet — but the company is betting that flexibility, not volume, is what modern manufacturing, and modern warfare, actually needs.In this series, our producer and host, Noelle Medina, gets an inside look at the small yet scaling companies quietly reinventing America's biggest industries.Check out our other episodes here: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLblFs6y75WUv7UtwrOApsHasI_YkauabF0:00 The four‑year replacement‑part problem0:38 Why traditional stamping dies make factories slow, rigid, and insanely expensive2:53 Ed Mehr’s path through SpaceX & Relativity Space 3:47 Founding Machina Labs to build a new kind of flexible, robot‑run factory5:30 Meet the RoboCraftsman7:12 Inside Mach 2: upgraded arms, swappable “warheads,” and containerized factory cells8:07 Two‑layer software & real‑time feedback that lets robots sculpt metal like human hands12:00 Where Machina actually wins13:03 Defense pivot15:53 Expressive customization and an off‑planet “teal workforce” futureGet the 5-minute newsletter keeping 2M+ innovators in the loop: https://thehustle.co/join-free-2

summary: The State Department notified Congress that it plans to sell Saudi Arabia up to 48 F-35 warplanes in a first-time sale that could be worth as much as $24.3 billion. The sale of the Lockheed Martin Corp. fighter jet to Saudi Arabia has been in the works for a number of years. President Donald Trump signaled in November the US would sell F-35s to the Kingdom, offering Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman a prize he's long cherished, ahead of a visit to the White House that month. Meantime, the Pentagon and Lockheed Martin Corp. are moving to speed up the production of a new classified air-to-air missile for US Air Force and Navy jets that's seen as vital to deterring China. For more, we speak with Wayne Sanders, Senior Defense Research Analyst for Bloomberg Intelligence.

At the heart of the agreement is the deployment of an IBM Quantum System Two, the latest generation of the company’s flagship quantum computer, which will be accessible to academics, researchers, and enterprises in the country.  The IBM system will be deployed at the Swiss National Supercomputing Center, which is affiliated with ETH Zurich, a prominent public research university.

title: US stocks end mixed, trading volatile amid Iran conflict
summary: STORY: U.S. stocks ended narrowly mixed after a volatile session on Monday, with the Dow ticking down marginally, the S&P 500 ending close to flat and the Nasdaq adding just over a third of a percent.Shares dropped early following weekend U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran.But bargain-hunting investors bought on dips as the day went on, showing an expectation that the disruptions from the conflict will be limited.Defense shares got a boost, with Lockheed Martin and Palantir Technologies gaining more than 3% and 5%, respectively.Joseph Shaposhnik is founder and CEO of Rainwater Equity."I believe the backdrop of this conflict continues to be supportive of our thesis, which is that we're in a defense supercycle. Clearly, European countries will be investing hundreds and hundreds of billions of dollars more over the next ten years to reach their defense targets as a percentage of GDP. Clearly, the US defense budget is going to significantly increase over the next couple of years and certainly this conflict is catalyzing investor interest in defense stocks, which we think have quite long legs over the next couple of years."Among other gainers, energy companies, whose profits rise alongside oil prices, outperformed, with shares of Exxon Mobil and Chevron both closing higher.On the downside, travel and airline stocks sank due to flight cancellations, higher jet fuel costs and widespread Middle East airspace closures.Shares of Carnival tumbled more than 7.5%, while JetBlue lost more than 5.5%, with Delta, American and United Airlines all also closing lower.Other notable stock moves included AES Corp, which plummeted more than 17%, after a consortium led by BlackRock-owned Global Infrastructure Partners and equity firm EQT AB agreed to acquire the utilities company for more than $33 billion.The sharp move lower suggested shareholders were disappointed with the $15-a-share price, which represented a 13% discount to AES' last close on Friday.
